frozen_original.title: Trump Withdraws from WHO and UNESCO, Abandoning Global Health Leadership
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed executive orders withdrawing the United States from the World Health Organization and UNESCO, repeating and expanding his first-term withdrawals that the Biden administration had reversed. The WHO withdrawal removed the United States from critical global disease surveillance networks just as public health experts warned of new pandemic risks. Global health officials warned the withdrawal would hamper international response to emerging infectious diseases. UNESCO partners expressed concern about the loss of U.S. leadership in global education and cultural heritage preservation. The double withdrawal signaled a broader retreat from multilateral institutions and international norms-based order.

children.title: Trump Orders U.S. Withdrawal from the World Health Organization
children.description_short: A Jan. 20, 2025 order directs steps toward U.S. withdrawal from WHO; it does not say membership ended that day.
children.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order stating that the United States intended to withdraw from the World Health Organization. It directed officials to pause future U.S. transfers, recall and reassign personnel, identify partners for necessary WHO activities, and cease negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement while withdrawal was in progress. The order does not establish that membership ended on January 20.
children.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order stating that the United States intended to withdraw from the World Health Organization. It directed the Secretary of State and Office of Management and Budget to pause future U.S. funds, support and resources to WHO; recall and reassign government personnel or contractors working with the organization; and identify U.S. and international partners to assume necessary WHO activities. The order also directed the Secretary of State to cease negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement and amendments to the International Health Regulations while withdrawal was in progress. This is an order to pursue withdrawal, not proof that the United States left WHO on January 20. The frozen entry incorrectly said the country withdrew from both WHO and UNESCO that day; the UNESCO action is a separate later claim and is kept in a second internal draft. The order's text does not establish the broader outcome claims in the frozen synopsis, so this card does not state that U.S. departure had already removed the country from disease-surveillance networks or produced quantified public-health harms.

children.title: U.S. UNESCO Withdrawal Decision Reported for July 2025 (Unverified)
children.description_short: Prior research says the U.S. chose to leave UNESCO in July 2025, with departure set for December 2026; the cited page could not be checked.
children.description_medium: According to the supplied packet, UNESCO Director-General Audrey Azoulay announced a U.S. decision to withdraw on July 22, 2025, effective at the end of December 2026. The cited UNESCO page returned an automated human-verification screen and could not be checked. A February 4 White House order required a review of UNESCO membership, not an immediate withdrawal; the July claim remains unverified and this draft is not publication-eligible.
children.description_long: The supplied research packet attributes a July 22, 2025 announcement to UNESCO Director-General Audrey Azoulay and says the United States had decided to withdraw from UNESCO, with departure to take effect at the end of December 2026. Those supplied details correct the frozen entry's January 20 date and distinguish a future withdrawal from a completed exit. The cited UNESCO statement could not be inspected during this review: a direct request returned an automated human-verification screen, while the connected Exa service returned an authorization error and Firecrawl reported that its credits were exhausted. The White House's February 4 order, which was fetched directly, says only that the United States would review its UNESCO membership within 90 days; it does not establish a July withdrawal decision or an enacted departure. This internal draft therefore preserves the supplied chronology for review, labels the central announcement and effective date unverified, and does not state that the United States has already left UNESCO. The original January 20 date is not supported for this UNESCO claim. Publication requires an accessible source excerpt confirming the announcement and timing.

primary.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an order stating that the United States intended to withdraw from the World Health Organization and directing prospective funding and personnel changes. The supplied materials describe a separate UNESCO withdrawal announcement on July 22, with withdrawal expected at the end of December 2026, while a February 4 order called for a review. The UNESCO statement could not be read, so those details remain unverified. The frozen record combines different dates and actions.
primary.description_long:
On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order stating that the United States intended to withdraw from the World Health Organization. The order directed officials to pause future U.S. funding and support, recall or reassign personnel and contractors working with WHO, identify partners for necessary activities, and stop negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement and amendments to the International Health Regulations while withdrawal was in progress. The order does not say that U.S. membership ended that day, and this draft makes no claim about resulting health effects.

The frozen record also says the United States withdrew from UNESCO on January 20. The supplied research materials instead place a separate UNESCO withdrawal announcement on July 22, 2025, with an effective date at the end of December 2026, and describe the February 4, 2025 executive order as directing a review of U.S. support to international organizations. Those UNESCO details remain unverified here: the cited page returned a human-verification screen, and the supplied account does not independently prove the announcement or effective date. This internal draft separates the events and marks the UNESCO claim as unverified. The parent remains ineligible for publication.

It directed officials to pause future U.S. transfers, recall and reassign personnel, identify partners for necessary WHO activities, and cease negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement while withdrawal was in progress. The order does not establish that membership ended on January 20.
children.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order stating that the United States intended to withdraw from the World Health Organization. It directed the Secretary of State and Office of Management and Budget to pause future U.S. funds, support and resources to WHO; recall and reassign government personnel or contractors working with the organization; and identify U.S. and international partners to assume necessary WHO activities. The order also directed the Secretary of State to cease negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement and amendments to the International Health Regulations while withdrawal was in progress. This is an order to pursue withdrawal, not proof that the United States left WHO on January 20. The frozen entry incorrectly said the country withdrew from both WHO and UNESCO that day; the UNESCO action is a separate later claim and is kept in a second internal draft. The order's text does not establish the broader outcome claims in the frozen synopsis, so this card does not state that U.S. departure had already removed the country from disease-surveillance networks or produced quantified public-health harms.

source_fact_map.fact: The Jan. 20 order states that the United States intends to withdraw from WHO.
source_fact_map.quote: The United States intends to withdraw from the WHO.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The White House January 20, 2025. WITHDRAWING THE UNITED STATES FROM THE WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION. Sec. 2. Actions. (a) The United States intends to withdraw from the WHO. The Presidential Letter to the Secretary-General of the United Nations signed on January 20, 2021, that retracted the United States’ July 6, 2020, notification of withdrawal is revoked.

source_fact_map.fact: The order directs officials to pause future transfers and reassign personnel or contractors working with WHO.
source_fact_map.quote: pause the future transfer of any United States Government funds, support, or resources to the WHO
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The Secretary of State and the Director of the Office of Management and Budget shall take appropriate measures, with all practicable speed, to: (i) pause the future transfer of any United States Government funds, support, or resources to the WHO; (ii) recall and reassign United States Government personnel or contractors working in any capacity with the WHO; and (iii) identify credible and transparent United States and international partners to assume necessary activities previously undertaken by the WHO.

source_fact_map.fact: The order directs the Secretary of State to cease negotiations while withdrawal is in progress.
source_fact_map.quote: While withdrawal is in progress, the Secretary of State will cease negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement and the amendments to the International Health Regulations
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Sec. 4. Global System Negotiations. While withdrawal is in progress, the Secretary of State will cease negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement and the amendments to the International Health Regulations, and actions taken to effectuate such agreement and amendments will have no binding force on the United States.

frozen_original.title: Tom Homan Border Czar Oversees ICE Raids in Churches and Schools
frozen_original.synopsis: Border Czar Tom Homan directed ICE to conduct enforcement raids in churches, schools, hospitals, and other previously protected sensitive locations, ending longstanding humanitarian protections that had been in place under administrations of both parties for decades. The raids terrorized immigrant communities across the country, caused children to be separated from parents, and forced undocumented people to avoid hospitals and churches out of fear of deportation. Human rights organizations documented hundreds of cases of collateral harm to U.S. citizens affected by the raids.

primary.title: DHS Rescinds Protected-Areas Guidance for Immigration Enforcement
primary.description_short: Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman rescinded 2021 guidance limiting immigration enforcement in or near protected areas.
primary.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman issued a memorandum rescinding the 2021 guidance for immigration enforcement in or near protected areas. DHS said the change applied to ICE and CBP and directed officers to use enforcement discretion without the prior bright-line rules. This supports a policy change, not claims that Tom Homan personally ordered raids or that specific collateral harms occurred.
primary.description_long: On January 20, 2025, Acting Department of Homeland Security Secretary Benjamine C. Huffman issued an immediate memorandum titled “Enforcement Actions in or Near Protected Areas.” The memo superseded and rescinded the October 27, 2021 DHS guidance for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection actions in or near areas previously designated for special protection. The memo says officers should continue using enforcement discretion and states that agency heads need not create “bright line rules” about where immigration laws may be enforced. DHS described the change as rescinding the Biden administration’s guidelines for enforcement in or near “sensitive” areas, including schools and churches. These records establish a change to department policy and expanded discretion at those locations. They do not establish that Border Czar Tom Homan personally ordered raids at churches or schools, how many such operations occurred, that families were separated as a result, or that advocates documented hundreds of collateral-harm cases. This entry is limited to the documented rescission and avoids turning a change in enforcement guidance into an unsupported account of specific raids or outcomes.

January 20,2025

MEMORANDUM FOR: Caleb Vitello

Acting Director U.S.Immigration and Customs Enforcement

Pete R.Flores

Senior Official Performing the Duties of the Commissioner U.S. Customs and Border Protection

FROM: Benjamine C. Huffman Acting Secretary

SUBJECT: Enforcement Actions in or Near Protected Areas

This memorandum addresses Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) enforcement actions in or near areas that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) previously determined require special protection. It is effective immediately. This memorandum supersedes and rescinds Alejandro Mayorkas's October 27, 2021 memorandum entitled, Guidelines for Enforcement Actions in or Near Protected Areas.

source_fact_map.fact: The memo no longer required agency heads to create bright-line rules governing where immigration enforcement may occur.
source_fact_map.quote: It is not necessary, however, for the head of the agency to create bright line rules regarding where our immigration laws are permitted to be enforced.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Going forward, law enforcement officers should continue to use that discretion along with a healthy dose of common sense. It is not necessary, however, for the head of the agency to create bright line rules regarding where our immigration laws are permitted to be enforced. The Director of ICE and the Commissioner of CBP may wish to issue further guidance to assist officers in exercising appropriate enforcement discretion.

source_fact_map.fact: DHS described the memo as rescinding Biden-era ICE and CBP enforcement guidance in or near sensitive areas.
source_fact_map.quote: The first directive rescinds the Biden Administration’s guidelines for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) enforcement actions that thwart law enforcement in or near so-called “sensitive” areas.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
Release Date: January 21, 2025

WASHINGTON – Yesterday, Acting Department of Homeland Security Secretary Benjamine Huffman issued two directives. The first directive rescinds the Biden Administration’s guidelines for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) enforcement actions that thwart law enforcement in or near so-called “sensitive” areas.

source_fact_map.fact: DHS's statement specifically mentioned schools and churches as locations where enforcement could occur.
source_fact_map.quote: Criminals will no longer be able to hide in America’s schools and churches to avoid arrest.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The following statement is attributable to a DHS Spokesperson: “This action empowers the brave men and women in CBP and ICE to enforce our immigration laws and catch criminal aliens—including murders and rapists—who have illegally come into our country. Criminals will no longer be able to hide in America’s schools and churches to avoid arrest. The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement, and instead trusts them to use common sense.”

frozen_original.title: Trump signs executive order allowing warrantless surveillance of political opponents
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump signed a sweeping executive order authorizing surveillance of political opponents without warrants, bypassing Fourth Amendment protections and enabling unprecedented government monitoring of dissidents. The order invoked broad national security justifications to authorize surveillance activities that would normally require judicial approval. Civil liberties advocates and constitutional law experts immediately challenged the order as a fundamental violation of the Fourth Amendment and the separation of powers.

primary.title: Unverified Draft: Alleged April 2025 Warrantless Surveillance Order
primary.description_short: Internal draft: the alleged April 2025 order authorizing warrantless surveillance of political opponents is unsupported by an identified order or source.
primary.description_medium: The frozen synopsis alleges Trump signed an April 2025 executive order permitting warrantless surveillance of political opponents and says civil-liberties advocates challenged it. The packet gives no order text, number, White House notice, named target, challenger or case. The signing, surveillance authority and reported challenge remain unverified.
primary.description_long: The frozen synopsis alleges President Donald Trump signed an executive order in April 2025 authorizing surveillance of political opponents without warrants under a broad national-security rationale. It says the measure bypassed Fourth Amendment protections and was immediately challenged by civil-liberties advocates and constitutional experts. This internal draft preserves those statements only as supplied allegations. The packet provides no order number or text, White House announcement, legal authority, implementing agency, surveillance target, named challenger or court case. It therefore does not establish that an order was signed, that surveillance occurred, or that a legal challenge followed. Related supplied records make different allegations: entry-6440 is dated March 2025 and refers to an order or internal guidance overriding FISA, while entry-6789 concerns alleged FISA Court judge changes and surveillance approvals in March. Those different dates, instruments and actions do not prove the April claim and are not substituted for it or merged with it. Until an April order is identified, neither the claimed authorization nor its legal and civil-liberties consequences can be stated as fact. April 1 remains the frozen input date, not a verified signing date.
primary.date_basis: Frozen input date retained for internal drafting; no executive order or signing date verified.
uncertainties: No April 2025 order, directive or source is identified in the supplied packet.

related_record_assessment.comparison: Entry-6440 is dated 2025-03-01 and alleges an order or guidance overriding FISA; entry-6789 is dated 2025-03-01 and alleges FISA Court judge changes and surveillance approvals. Entry-6928 is dated 2025-04-01 and alleges a separate order. No same-event evidence is supplied; the differing dates and mechanisms are retained and no merge is proposed.
